extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of English literary history; people studying 18th-century periodical essays and satire
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for composing short, periodical essays in the manner of the Tatler/Spectator—light, moral, accessible pieces that influence public taste without rancor. Covers tone, audience, use of facts, persona, frequency, and moral purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure actions, not persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper's business is 'to censure the Actions of Men, not of Parties' and 'They do not design to expose Persons but things'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim satire and criticism at vices, follies, and actions rather than personal scandal; only expose those 'more than ordinarily deserve it.' This preserves moral authority and avoids mere personal attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Little Diversion' at the end of papers
rubrics_metrics.description: After serious matters are over, append 'a little Diversion ... as anything occurs to make the World Merry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure pieces so that a lighter, amusing item follows weightier argument — a deliberate mixing of serious commentary with small amusements to engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep pieces short and accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: 'many men care but for a little reading at a time ... thus we wheedle them ... to the Knowledge of the World.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write concise, digestible essays because the broad public prefers short reading; shortness and clarity widen readership and 'wheedle' less-engaged readers into learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain earnestness within a cheerful, unpretending tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Restraint of deep earnestness 'within the bounds of a cheerful, unpretending influence. Drop by drop it should fall, and its strength lie in its persistence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance moral seriousness with a light, modest voice; influence is more effective when gradual and steady rather than strident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantry and appeals to passion
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer 'would affect no pedantry of moralizing, he would appeal to no passions, he would profess himself only "a Tatler."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eschew scholarly pedantry and emotional manipulation. Maintain a modest persona that refrains from high-flown moralizing or sensational appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct wit toward useful ends
rubrics_metrics.description: 'wit, if a man had it, unless it be directed to some useful end, is but a wanton, frivolous quality' — value wit that has an 'honourable intention'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humor and wit instrumentally to promote virtue, good sense, or social improvement rather than mere cleverness for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associate grace and kindliness with everyday incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Exquisite grace and true kindliness, here associated with familiar ways and common incidents of everyday life' make the writing appealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground essays in commonplace situations and ordinary life, using a graceful, kindly tone to make moral points relatable and appealing to a wide audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make learning amiable and attractive
rubrics_metrics.description: The periodical 'rescued' learning from pedants and 'discovered the true method of making it amiable and lovely to all mankind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present ideas and instruction attractively so that learning becomes enjoyable; avoid didactic, off-putting modes that alienate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume a reasonable, common-sense reader and use gentle humor
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A sense of the essentials of life was assumed everywhere for the reader, who was asked only to smile charitably at its vanities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presume an intelligent, decent reader and employ a charitable, tolerant humor that invites a smile rather than ridicule; gentle satire encourages self-improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain influence by persistence and regular publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The tactic that 'Drop by drop it should fall, and its strength lie in its persistence' and the contrast of thrice-weekly Tatlers vs. daily Spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent, regular publication (daily or frequent issues) to create a sustained influence and a familiar voice readers return to; schedule and frequency shape tone and manageability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor essays in contemporaneous facts and news
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'some of the news obtained by virtue of the office of Gazetteer ... to bring weight and acceptance' to the writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate current events or verifiable facts to lend authority and topicality, enhancing credibility and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a persona or pseudonym where useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele and others wrote under personae (e.g., Isaac Bickerstaff) to carry on jests and critique superstition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A consistent persona can frame satire, permit sustained jokes, and create reader familiarity; use pseudonymous characters to embody a voice or viewpoint without personal invective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political engagement without personality
rubrics_metrics.description: When acting politically (e.g., in the 'Guardian' or 'Englishman'), Steele maintained 'unexampled abstinence from personality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate political positions and defend rights but avoid personal attacks on opponents; principled, impersonal argument preserves moral standing and broad appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of subjects handled with consistent quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors treated a 'vast variety of subjects ... in so different manners, and yet all so perfectly well.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover diverse topics and registers while maintaining consistent judgment, taste, and workmanship so readers trust the writer across subjects.
